title: The hermitage (1965)
hookLine: he moves to a cinderblock house in the woods
carry: a small house in the woods
tomorrow: the monk who spoke about war and race

cards: Everybody has a daydream about a cabin. A little place at the end of a dirt road. No commute, no inbox, just trees and a porch and a kettle.

For most people it stays a daydream. In August 1965, a fifty-year-old monk walked up a path through the Kentucky woods, about a mile from his abbey, to a plain cinderblock house with a fireplace and a porch.
He'd been asking for this for years. Now he'd live there, mostly alone.

teach.b: First, the word. Hermit comes from the Greek eremos, the desert.
The first Christian hermits went out into the deserts of Egypt and Syria in the third and fourth centuries, men and women like Saint Antony, looking for God in silence.
Merton loved them, and translated some of their sayings in a small book, The Wisdom of the Desert. Second, the house. It had been put up around 1960 for meetings with visitors from other churches.
Merton started spending afternoons there, then days, and in 1965 his abbot let him move in full time.
He chopped wood, hauled water, prayed the psalms, read and wrote. He still walked down to the abbey most days for Mass and a meal. Third, why a hermit, if he was already a monk?
Even a silent monastery is a busy place: schedules, jobs, hundreds of people, and by then Merton was well-known and swamped with visitors.
He wanted to go further into the solitude that had drawn him to Gethsemani in the first place. Fourth, the Gospel model. Jesus did this too.

teach.h: A DESERT PLACE, AND THERE HE PRAYED.
teach.b: In Mark, in the Douay-Rheims: "And rising very early, going out, he went into a desert place: and there he prayed." A hermitage is that desert place, made permanent.
And here's the surprise: Merton's hermitage years were some of his most connected. He wrote hundreds of letters from that porch, to poets, activists and religious teachers around the world.
Solitude didn't shrink his world. It widened it.

how: The Catholic Church recognizes hermits living under a bishop or within religious orders, and many monasteries have hermitages where monks or retreatants can spend days in solitude and prayer.

o: someone who lives mostly alone, to pray
someone who hides because they dislike people
a monk who wanders from town to town

p: an early desert hermit in Egypt

s: as a hermit, Merton cut off all contact with the world
he wrote hundreds of letters from the hermitage to people around the world.
hermit comes from the Greek word for desert
eremos: the desert where the first Christian hermits lived.
Jesus went off alone to pray
"he went into a desert place: and there he prayed."

games.q: you're a well-known monk, swamped with visitors and jobs, and you long for deeper solitude. what do you do?
o: ask, for years, to live alone in a small house nearby
games.why: Merton asked patiently for years, and in 1965 his abbot let him live full time in the hermitage near the abbey.

practice: You probably can't move to a cabin, but you can find a corner: a chair by a window, the steps outside, the car, parked, before you go in. Picture one spot that could be quiet, sit in it now in your mind, and let it become familiar.
If you pray, you can offer that corner to God as your desert place.

wordCard.voice: Hermit. From the Greek for desert: someone who lives mostly alone, to pray. Merton became one in 1965, in a cinderblock house in the Kentucky woods. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: desert, wilderness, the root of hermit.

carryVoice: Your line: a small house in the woods. A quiet corner can be one, too. Until tomorrow.
